title: What are the key metrics to measure — Response Time (how long one request takes), Throughput (requests per second), Error Rate (% of failed requests), Latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99 — p99 is more important than average)?
shortTitle: Key metrics to measure in performance testing

s1_definition.profdef: The key performance metrics are response time, how long a single request takes end to end; throughput, how many requests the system completes per second; error rate, the percentage of requests that fail; and latency percentiles such as the fiftieth, ninety-fifth, and ninety-ninth, which describe the distribution of response times. Percentiles matter more than the average because the average hides the slow tail that real users experience, so the ninety-ninth percentile, the slowest one percent, is often more important than the mean when judging user experience and meeting service-level objectives.
s1_definition.analogy: When the National Bank of India measures its transfer service under load, response time is how long one customer waits for a transfer to confirm, throughput is how many transfers the system finishes each second, and error rate is the share of transfers that fail. Latency percentiles describe the spread of waiting times: the fiftieth percentile is the typical customer, the ninety-fifth is a fairly unlucky customer, and the ninety-ninth is the unluckiest one in a hundred. The average is misleading, because if ninety-nine customers wait fifty milliseconds and one waits ten seconds, the average still looks fine, but that one furious customer, the ninety-ninth percentile, is the real experience you must control. So the bank watches the tail, not just the average.
s1_definition.oneliner: Measure response time per request, throughput as requests per second, error rate as the percentage that fail, and latency percentiles p50, p95, and p99, and judge against percentiles rather than the average because the average hides the slow tail that real users feel.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The key performance metrics are response time, how long a single request takes end to end; throughput, how many requests the system completes per second; error rate, the percentage of requests that fail; and latency percentiles such as the fiftieth, ninety-fifth, and ninety-ninth, which describe the distribution of response times. Percentiles matter more than the average because the average hides the slow tail that real users experience, so the ninety-ninth percentile, the slowest one percent, is often more important than the mean when judging user experience and meeting service-level objectives.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the National Bank of India measures its transfer service under load, response time is how long one customer waits for a transfer to confirm, throughput is how many transfers the system finishes each second, and error rate is the share of transfers that fail. Latency percentiles describe the spread of waiting times: the fiftieth percentile is the typical customer, the ninety-fifth is a fairly unlucky customer, and the ninety-ninth is the unluckiest one in a hundred. The average is misleading, because if ninety-nine customers wait fifty milliseconds and one waits ten seconds, the average still looks fine, but that one furious customer, the ninety-ninth percentile, is the real experience you must control. So the bank watches the tail, not just the average.

**One line to remember:** Measure response time per request, throughput as requests per second, error rate as the percentage that fail, and latency percentiles p50, p95, and p99, and judge against percentiles rather than the average because the average hides the slow tail that real users feel.

sections.s2_technical:
Response time is the end-to-end duration of a single request from send to full response, and it is the most direct measure of user-perceived speed. You rarely report a single response-time number because requests vary; instead you summarize the distribution. Throughput is the rate of completed requests, typically requests or transactions per second, and it measures capacity, how much work the system actually processes. Throughput and response time interact: as load rises, throughput increases until the system saturates, after which throughput plateaus or falls while response time climbs, so you read them together to find the capacity knee. Error rate is the fraction of requests that fail, whether by error status, timeout, or dropped connection, and it is critical because a system that is fast only because it is rejecting requests is not actually performing; error rate must stay within an acceptable bound for the latency numbers to be meaningful.

Latency percentiles describe the shape of the response-time distribution. The fiftieth percentile, the median, is the typical experience, half of requests are faster and half slower. The ninety-fifth percentile is the value below which ninety-five percent of requests fall, capturing a fairly bad experience. The ninety-ninth percentile is the value below which ninety-nine percent fall, capturing the slow tail, the worst one in a hundred. Percentiles matter more than the average because averages are dominated by the bulk and hide outliers: a distribution with a few very slow requests can have a healthy-looking average while a meaningful fraction of users suffer badly, and in a high-traffic bank one percent of requests is a large absolute number of real customers. The ninety-ninth percentile is therefore often the metric that governs user experience and service-level objectives, and some systems even watch the ninety-ninth-point-nine for the extreme tail. A related trap is averaging percentiles across time windows or servers, which is mathematically invalid; you must compute percentiles from the full distribution.

The metrics are interpreted together and against defined targets. A service-level objective typically states a percentile latency bound at a given throughput with a maximum error rate, for example ninety-fifth-percentile latency under two hundred milliseconds and error rate under one percent at the expected peak transactions per second. Under a performance test you watch all four as load increases: response-time percentiles and error rate rising sharply while throughput plateaus marks the capacity ceiling. The senior nuances are to always report percentiles, especially the tail, rather than averages, because the tail is what users feel and what breaches objectives; to read throughput and latency together to understand capacity; to treat error rate as a gate on the validity of latency, since fast-but-failing is not success; to compute percentiles over the real distribution rather than averaging them; and to tie every metric to a business-relevant target rather than reporting raw numbers. You also correlate client-side metrics with server-side resource metrics, CPU, memory, connection pools, so a latency spike can be traced to the saturating resource. In a bank the tail matters especially during predictable surges, because the slowest one percent during salary day can be tens of thousands of real customers, so controlling p99, not just the average, is what actually protects the customer experience and meets regulatory expectations for availability.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must judge its transfer service by what real customers feel, so it needs latency percentiles, not just an average, which is exactly p50, p95, and p99.

Problem 2 — It must read throughput and error rate alongside latency to know whether the service is truly performing or merely rejecting requests, which is exactly the combined interpretation.

Problem 3 — It must show how an average can look healthy while the ninety-ninth percentile is terrible, which is exactly the average-versus-tail lesson.

In the mini-project we compute all four metrics from a set of recorded response times including a slow tail, and show that the average looks fine while the ninety-ninth percentile breaches the target, making the point concrete. We write a Java harness.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

java -cp out com.bank.qa.metrics.PerfMetricsDemo

# Real tools report these automatically:
#   k6: http_req_duration{p(95),p(99)}, http_reqs (throughput), http_req_failed
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one hundred recorded response times, ninety-nine around fifty milliseconds and one at three thousand milliseconds, with two of the hundred failing.

Step 1: The calculator computes the average, which is dominated by the ninety-nine fast requests and comes out low, so by itself it looks healthy, which is the misleading signal.

Step 2: It computes the fiftieth percentile, the median, which is about fifty milliseconds, representing the typical customer who is served quickly.

Step 3: It computes the ninety-fifth percentile, still low because ninety-five of the hundred are fast, and then the ninety-ninth percentile, which jumps to three thousand milliseconds because it captures the slow tail, the worst one in a hundred, revealing the problem the average hid.

Step 4: It computes throughput as one hundred requests in one second and the error rate as two percent, so reading all four together shows the service is both tail-slow and over the error budget, not actually performing well.

Step 5: The service-level check fails on the ninety-ninth-percentile tail and the error rate even though the average looked fine, demonstrating concretely why percentiles, especially p99, matter more than the average when judging real user experience.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] === Key performance metrics (transfer API under load) ===
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] Average response time = 79ms  <-- looks fine, HIDES the tail
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] p50 (median) = 49ms
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] p95          = 54ms
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] p99          = 3000ms  <-- the slowest 1% real users feel
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] Throughput   = 100 req/s
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] Error rate   = 2.0%
2026-10-30 10:32:20 [INFO] SLA check (p95<200ms, p99<500ms, err<1%): BREACH (p99 tail and/or error rate fail — avg was misleading)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Recorded samples (response times + successes/failures)
    │
    ▼
  Compute metrics (from the FULL distribution):
    ├─ response time → percentiles p50 / p95 / p99
    ├─ throughput    → completed / window seconds
    └─ error rate    → failed / total %
    │
    ▼
  Average = low (hides tail)   vs   p99 = high (the slow 1% users feel)
    │
    ▼
  Judge against SLA: p95<200ms AND p99<500ms AND err<1%
    │  (fast-but-failing is NOT success → error rate gates latency)
    ▼
  Correlate with server CPU/mem/pool to find the saturating resource
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — The Four Key Metrics ═══

  ┌─ Metric → meaning → why ──────────────────────────────┐
  │ response time  : per-request duration (user-perceived)│
  │ throughput     : req/s completed (capacity)           │
  │ error rate     : % failed (gates latency validity)    │
  │ percentiles    : p50 typical, p95 bad, p99 slow tail  │
  │ AVERAGE hides the tail → judge by p95/p99             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Never average percentiles across windows/servers.

  ── State Diagram: rising load ──────────────────────────
  [throughput ↑, latency flat] → [knee] → [throughput flat,
   p99 ↑, errors ↑]  ← capacity ceiling

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. percentile(sorted, 50/95/99)
  2. throughputPerSec(completed, window)
  3. errorRatePct(failed, total)
  4. compare to SLO (tail + errors)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The key performance metrics I measure are response time, throughput, error rate, and latency percentiles. Response time is the end-to-end duration of a single request and the most direct measure of user-perceived speed, but I never report it as one number because requests vary; I summarize the distribution. Throughput is the rate of completed requests, requests or transactions per second, which measures capacity. Error rate is the fraction of requests that fail by error status, timeout, or dropped connection, and it is critical because a system that is fast only because it is rejecting requests is not performing, so the error rate gates the validity of the latency numbers. And latency percentiles describe the shape of the distribution: the fiftieth is the typical experience, the ninety-fifth a fairly bad one, and the ninety-ninth the slow tail, the worst one in a hundred.

The point I stress is that percentiles matter more than the average, because the average is dominated by the bulk and hides outliers. A distribution with a few very slow requests can show a healthy average while a meaningful fraction of users suffer badly, and in a high-traffic bank one percent of requests is a huge absolute number of real customers, so the ninety-ninth percentile is often the metric that actually governs user experience and the service-level objective. I also avoid the trap of averaging percentiles across time windows or servers, which is mathematically invalid, and I always compute them from the full distribution. I read the metrics together and against defined targets, a typical objective being ninety-fifth-percentile latency under two hundred milliseconds with error rate under one percent at the expected peak, and I watch throughput and latency together to find the capacity knee where throughput plateaus while latency and errors climb. I also correlate client-side latency with server-side resource metrics so a spike can be traced to the saturating resource.

At the National Bank of India this mattered acutely on salary day, where the slowest one percent of transfer requests could be tens of thousands of real customers, so I reported p95 and p99, not the average, and I remember a case where the average latency looked perfectly healthy while the p99 was several seconds because of a slow tail from a saturating connection pool, which only the percentile view and the error rate revealed. Being able to define the four metrics and explain why the tail percentiles beat the average, and why error rate gates latency, is what shows an interviewer I measure performance the way it actually affects customers rather than hiding behind a flattering average.
